newsitem.title: GREECE: Modern art museum not to cover Aristotle's Lyceum.
newsitem.headline: Modern art museum not to cover Aristotle's Lyceum.

text.p: The ruins of Aristotle's ancient Lyceum, discovered recently by Greek archaeologists in central Athens, will not be covered by a new modern art museum, the culture ministry said on Wednesday.

One of Athens' great Classical schools, the Lyceum was unearthed during excavations ahead of the museum's construction under a dirt car parking lot in the heart of Athens, about two km (1.2 miles) from the Acropolis.

Archaeologists hailed the discovery of the site as among the finds of the century, saying this was where Aristotle taught and wrote about politics, science and ethics, laying the foundations of Western thinking.
When announcing the find, Culture Minister Evangelos Venizelos said that efforts would be made so that the ruins could be incorporated into the museum's plans.
But Venizelos on Wednesday declared this impossible.

"Although co-existence is a solution that could have great architectural, aesthetic and cultural interest internationally, it would not serve the twin goal of best displaying a great archaeological find and quickly building a private museum," he said.
The museum, designed by Ieoh Ming Pei -- whose work includes the modern pyramid in the Louvre -- and funded by the Goulandris shipping family, must now be built elsewhere, he said.
Local residents had protested against the museum and demanded a park in the over-developed, expensive area where many embassies, galleries and museums are located.
But plans went ahead and preparatory digging revealed the major part of a 4th century BC wrestling arena, believed to be part of the Lyceum, under a sprawling gymnasium dating to Roman times.

Excavators said the arena was well preserved and offered a wide range of evidence indicating this was where Aristotle founded his Peripatetic School, named after the arcade where he liked to stroll and talk with small groups of students.
Aristotle, who lived between 384 and 322 BC, studied under Plato and taught Macedonian king Alexander the Great.
He founded his own school after leaving Plato's Academy, another of ancient Greece's great schools, where the sons of the Athenian elite trained both their minds and bodies.
Plato's Academy is located in what is now a run-down industrial district near central Athens.
